title: Discussing a DNACPR decision with a relative

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking
guidelineVersions: BMA, RC(UK), RCN Decisions relating to CPR (3rd ed., 1st revision, 2016)
GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010; updated Mar 2022 and Dec 2024)
R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014] EWCA Civ 822
Winspear v City Hospitals Sunderland [2015] EWHC 3250 (QB)

related.why: Advance decisions and refusal of treatment

brief.scenario: Mrs Edith Barraclough, 82, is day 5 after an emergency Hartmann's procedure for perforated diverticulitis. She has hospital-acquired pneumonia, is deteriorating despite treatment and lacks capacity because of delirium. Her consultant has assessed her and judges that CPR would not restart her heart. The consultant has asked you to discuss this with her daughter, Linda, before the decision is recorded, and will meet Linda later today.
brief.task: Discuss the DNACPR decision with Linda.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Consult and inform, not ask permission: explain why CPR would not work and that all other care continues.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Asking the daughter to decide, or letting her think care is being withdrawn.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Can you tell me what you understand about how your mum is doing?"

grid.label: Opening and understanding
grid.fail: Starts with "We're not going to resuscitate her" in the corridor.
grid.pass: Private room, introduces self and role, asks what she understands, gives a warning shot before difficult news.
grid.high: Asks about her mother as a person and what she would have wanted, before discussing CPR.

grid.label: Why CPR would not work
grid.fail: Uses jargon ("futile", "DNACPR") or blames her age.
grid.pass: Plain words: CPR is chest compressions, shocks and a breathing tube; with her illness it would not restart her heart.
grid.high: Explains the decision is about what will not work, not her worth; the consultant with lead responsibility made it.

grid.label: Other treatment continues
grid.pass: Antibiotics, oxygen, fluids, physiotherapy and nursing continue; the decision covers only CPR.
grid.high: Explains a separate plan for other treatments, often recorded on a ReSPECT form, and that comfort is always provided.

grid.label: Proxy and her mother's wishes
grid.fail: Does not ask about a health and welfare attorney or advance decision.
grid.pass: Asks about a health and welfare LPA, advance decision and her mother's wishes; explains her role is to advise, not decide.
grid.high: Explains why she is consulted: the patient cannot take part, and the law requires those close to her to be consulted.

grid.label: Handling disagreement
grid.fail: Agrees to CPR to avoid conflict, or argues with her.
grid.pass: Acknowledges distress; explains CPR that will not work is not offered even on request; offers consultant meeting and second opinion.
grid.high: Explores what she fears CPR would give her mother; keeps the door open without implying the clinical facts will change.

grid.label: Record and review
grid.fail: Makes no record, or presents the decision as permanent.
grid.pass: Records who was present, what was explained and her views; consultant completes the form; revisited if her condition changes.
grid.high: Tells her how to raise concerns, and that the decision is shared with the team and moves with her mother.

grid.label: Summary and support
grid.fail: Leaves without checking understanding or offering support.
grid.pass: Summarises, checks understanding, invites questions, explains next steps including the consultant's meeting.
grid.high: Offers practical support: open visiting, chaplaincy, contact details, and asks who else in the family should know.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hi, I'm one of the doctors. We've decided we're not going to resuscitate your mum.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: At her age CPR is futile.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Linda: "So you're giving up on her?"

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: We'll just keep her comfortable now.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: OK, if that's what you want, we'll keep her for CPR.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Right, I'll let you get back to her.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors caring for your mum. Shall we sit down? What do you understand about how she's doing? I'm afraid I have some difficult news.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Her pneumonia is getting worse despite treatment. If her heart stopped, CPR means pressing hard on the chest, electric shocks and a breathing tube. Her consultant's judgement is that, with this illness, it would not restart her heart.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Linda: "So you're giving up on her?"

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No. She'll keep having antibiotics, oxygen, fluids, physiotherapy and nursing care. This decision is only about CPR.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Did your mum ever make a lasting power of attorney for health, or a written advance decision? What would she have wanted? You're not being asked to decide, but your view matters.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I can see how hard this is. We won't offer CPR that won't work, even if asked, but your mum's consultant will meet you today, and you can have a second opinion.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll record our conversation and your views. The consultant will complete the form, and it will be looked at again if her condition changes.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can I check what you've taken from this? Any questions?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors. Before we talk about treatment, tell me about your mum. What was she like, and did she ever say what she'd want if she became very ill?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Linda: "She hated fuss. But she's a fighter."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This isn't about her age or her worth. Her consultant, who leads her care, has judged CPR would not work because of how severe this infection is.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: We'll also agree a plan for her other treatments and write it on a ReSPECT form. Whatever happens, we'll keep her comfortable.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Because your mum can't talk with us herself, we must hear from you first. You know her best.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: When you say 'everything', what do you hope CPR would do for her? I'd be worried it would hurt her without bringing her back.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If you have concerns later, speak to the nurse in charge or ask for the consultant. The decision goes wherever she goes, and everyone caring for her knows it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You can visit at any time, and the chaplain is available. Is there anyone else in the family we should speak to?

failures.move: Agreeing to CPR because the daughter insists.
failures.consequence: Exposes her mother to a harmful procedure that will not work; relatives cannot demand it (BMA/RC(UK)/RCN 2016; GMC para 134).

failures.move: Letting her believe DNACPR means stopping treatment.
failures.consequence: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR (GMC para 143); misunderstanding destroys trust.

failures.move: Recording the decision without consulting the family.
failures.consequence: Unlawful unless consultation is not practicable or appropriate (Winspear 2015; GMC para 136).

failures.move: Presenting it as a decision based on her age.
failures.consequence: The decision rests on her clinical state; age alone is not a reason.

recovery.when: She says "So you're asking me to decide?"
recovery.line: No. You don't have to carry that. We need to know what your mum would have wanted; the medical decision rests with her consultant.
I can see how upsetting this is. Would it help if I explained again, more slowly?

knowledge.fact: If CPR will not succeed, the person with lead responsibility may decide not to attempt it; discuss sensitively (para 134).
If the patient lacks capacity, consult any legal proxy and those close to her about the decision and reasons, unless not practicable or appropriate (para 136).
Failure to involve a patient with capacity in a DNACPR decision breached Article 8.
Futility alone does not excuse failing to consult the family of a patient who lacks capacity.
A health and welfare attorney can refuse life-sustaining treatment only if the LPA expressly allows it.

recall.think: She may arrest soon; CPR would not work and would harm her.
recall.say: "This decision is only about CPR. All her other care continues."
do: Ask what she knows and about her mum
Explain why CPR would not work
Ask about LPA and wishes; record

numbers.meaning: consult proxy and those close if she lacks capacity

recall.finish: Consultant meets the daughter; record; revisit if her condition changes.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format; communication stations with a role player

sources.name: GMC: Treatment and care towards the end of life: good practice in decision making
sources.version: In effect 1 July 2010; updated 15 March 2022 and 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Consult those close to a patient lacking capacity (para 133); when CPR will not succeed, the person with lead responsibility judges and it must be sensitively discussed (para 134); consult any legal proxy and those close about the DNACPR decision and reasons (para 136); proxy requesting CPR: explore reasons, explain, right to a second opinion (para 140); DNACPR applies only to CPR (para 143)

sources.name: BMA, Resuscitation Council (UK) and Royal College of Nursing: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation
sources.supports: CPR that will not succeed should not be attempted; relatives are informed and consulted but cannot demand it; DNACPR does not affect other treatment; decisions recorded, communicated and revisited when circumstances change

sources.name: Resuscitation Council UK: ReSPECT (Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment), version 3
sources.supports: Recording recommendations about CPR and other emergency treatment in the context of an overall care plan; prompts to involve family or proxy when the patient lacks capacity

sources.name: R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust [2014] EWCA Civ 822
sources.supports: Article 8 requires involving a patient with capacity in a DNACPR decision unless that would cause physical or psychological harm

sources.name: Winspear v City Hospitals Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust [2015] EWHC 3250 (QB)
sources.supports: Where the patient lacks capacity, those close to the patient must be consulted before a DNACPR notice is made unless not practicable or appropriate; clinical futility alone is not a reason not to consult

sources.name: Mental Capacity Act 2005 (c. 9)
sources.supports: Best interests: consult those close to the person (s4(7)); an attorney may refuse life-sustaining treatment only if the LPA expressly authorises it (s11(7)–(8)); advance decisions (ss24–26)

partner.opening: Linda is in the relatives' room. Please begin.
partner.actorBrief: You are Linda Barraclough, 54, a pharmacy assistant, Edith's only daughter. You live nearby and visit daily. You know your mum had an emergency bowel operation and 'a chest infection', but think she is improving. There is no lasting power of attorney or advance decision. Your mum once said, after your father's death in intensive care, that she 'didn't want all those tubes'. Opening line: "Is Mum getting better? The nurse said you wanted a word." Emotional state: tired, then shocked and angry. Hidden concern: you feel guilty that you encouraged her to have the operation. Say "Are you saying you're giving up on her?" if the candidate mentions CPR without explaining. Later say "I want everything done" once. If asked what your mum was like or what she would have wanted, soften and share the comment about tubes. If the candidate is kind and clear, accept the decision but ask to see the consultant.

reveals.trigger: Asks what her mother would have wanted
reveals.finding: "After Dad died in intensive care, she said she didn't want all those tubes."

reveals.trigger: Asks about LPA or advance decision

reveals.finding: "I told her to have the operation. Did I do this to her?"

push.question: What would you say if she asks you to do everything?
push.expect: Explore what she hopes for; CPR that will not work is not offered; all other treatment continues; consultant meeting and second opinion.

push.question: What if she disagrees with the decision?
push.expect: Acknowledge; consultant discussion; second opinion; record her views; decision revisited if condition changes.

curveballs.prompt: "Did I do this to her by telling her to have the operation?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Without the operation she would very likely have died; she needed it, and supporting her was the right thing to do.

curveballs.prompt: "She has a health and welfare LPA and I'm her attorney. I refuse to let you put this on her notes."
curveballs.safeAnswer: An attorney can refuse treatment but cannot demand CPR that will not work; consult her fully, involve the consultant, offer a second opinion.
Acknowledge her distress, explain the reasons again, arrange the consultant meeting and second opinion, and tell her how to raise concerns (PALS).
